meaning.evidence: Every fact kept: the sale, the old man's advice, Doyle scouting, the Grand Rapids games, Flynn's misjudged fly. "I didn't have no idea nothing like that was on the cards" matches.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "big-noting meself" for boasting, "running the eye over me" for looking me over, "on song" for when I was right, "the guts" for nerve.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a real bush-league yarn: "happy as Larry", "having a squiz", "not all up meself", "Say g'day to all the boys".

register.evidence: Level 3: steady Aussie idiom on top of Jack's grammar ("Fair dinkum Al it come as a shock"), no swearing beyond the brief.

tone.evidence: Jack's naive, boastful-modest letter voice survives, misspellings and all ("appresiated", "that serious", "excepted").

flow.evidence: Reads naturally: "I can't help being proud of me first year's record in professional baseball".

variety.evidence: Good spread; "mate" recurs (salutation, "old mate", "mates", "Your mate"), as the original's "pal" did.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably Ring Lardner's Jack Keefe, now with an Aussie tongue.

problems.why: Odd as a letter salutation; Australians would still write "Dear Al" or keep "Friend".
Fine, but loses the period slang "birds" for no gain.

A.summary: A clean, natural level-3 retelling that keeps Jack's voice and misspellings.

meaning.evidence: Adds lines that change Jack's confidence: "Buggered if I know." after the tall-buildings boast and "Well, I'll be buggered." after the sign-off; otherwise intact.

sense.evidence: "all you beaut old pals" and "They always was beaut to me" strain; "won't have sweet bugger-all on you" is a forced swap.

authenticity.evidence: Swaps bolted onto the untouched original: "that bloody big league", "this bloody big league business", "FRIEND AL: Well, Al old pal".

register.evidence: Lighter than level 3 in substance (most sentences unchanged: "I will just give them what I got"), with swearing tacked on; "bloody", "bugger" within dad.

tone.evidence: The tacked-on oaths make the guileless Jack sound coarse and doubtful ("Buggered if I know.").

flow.evidence: Jarring joins: "Your mate, JACK. Well, I'll be buggered."

variety.evidence: Leans on "bloody", "bugger" and "beaut" over and over.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the letter, since most of it is the original.

problems.why: Added line undercuts Jack's cocky "eh Al?".

problems.quote: Your mate, JACK. Well, I'll be buggered.
problems.why: Oath after the signature; nonsensical in a letter.
"beaut" as an adjective for people is forced.
Bolted-on "bloody" in the old man's speech.

problems.quote: I will just give them what I got
problems.original: I will just give them what I got
problems.why: Large stretches left untranslated for a level-3 brief.

B.summary: Mostly the original with oaths and "beaut" bolted on, including added lines that change the tone.

meaning.evidence: All facts kept; small colour like "they only got one run" and "the young fellas on the team" hangs off the original.

sense.evidence: Mostly exact ("a bit of ticker", "never had Buckley's", "sussing me out"), but "show them galahs" turns neutral birds into fools, and "the fair go I got" shifts treatment.

authenticity.evidence: Natural idiom: "never had Buckley's against me when I was on song", "happy as Larry", "not skiting".

register.evidence: Level 3, consistently retold, no swearing beyond "bugger all", within dad.

tone.evidence: Keeps Jack's naive bravado and his misspellings ("appresiated", "that serious").

flow.evidence: Mostly smooth, with some mixing of forms: "So I says I would do me best".

variety.evidence: Wide range of idiom, but "fair dinkum" twice and "on the cards"/"on song" close together.

problems.why: "galahs" means fools; adds a sneer to the old man's neutral "birds".
"fair go" is a slightly different idea from treatment.

problems.quote: fair dinkum Al I will make good
problems.original: believe me Al I will make good

C.summary: Lively and natural, nearly level with A; a couple of terms shift sense slightly.
